stories.headline: Elusive peace: On Kashmir terror attack
stories.title: Elusive peace: On Kashmir terror attack
stories.summary: Restoration of Statehood is essential for peace in Jammu and Kashmir
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'terror attack' in title weight 84
article_sentences: Three months of lull established by security forces in Jammu and Kashmir was rattled by the back-to-back incidents of violence in the past six days.
On November 11, a terror attack on a checkpoint manned by the personnel of the Central Reserve.
Police Force (CRPF) in Kulgam left three jawans injured.
On November 16, a local, whom the police suspected of having joined the terror ranks a few days ago, was killed after six days of a siege-like anti-terror operation in residential areas of Kulgam.
In Jammu’s Kishtwar, two Special.
Police Officers (SPOs) of the J&K. Police were found dead with bullet wounds, a day after they were reported missing in a forest range on November 11.
The police and the Army, however, remain tight-lipped about the circumstances around the killing of these SPOs, and there are conflicting reports on the circumstances that led to their deaths.
The anti-terror operation in civilian areas of Kulgam has raised concerns.

Former J&K Chief Minister and PDP president Mehbooba Mufti described the operation, spread over six days, as “collective punishment that only breeds alienation and resentment,” while NC spokesman Imran Nabi Dar suggested that entire villages were put under prolonged restrictions for days.
The Omar Abdullah government, because of limited powers and no jurisdiction over the police in J&K, a Union Territory since 2019, finds itself hamstrung.
The iron hand policy to stamp out terrorism and separatism has been effective from a strictly security perspective — terror attacks as well as local recruitments into terror ranks have declined.
According to the police, local recruits have come down to single digit or fewer than 10 in Kashmir.

stories.headline: CM Chandrababu Naidu seeks Centre bailout as 2 cyclones cost AP Rs 7k cr
stories.title: CM Chandrababu Naidu seeks Centre bailout as 2 cyclones cost AP Rs 7k cr
stories.summary: Naidu meets FM in Delhi, discusses cyclone damage Farm losses, battered coastal infra figure in talks Seeks funds for Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub, VER
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: Amaravati: Chief Minister N Chandrababu Naidu has appealed to Union Finance Minister Nirmala Sitharaman for immediate financial assistance to Andhra Pradesh, which suffered losses exceeding Rs 7,000 crore due to two successive cyclones, Arnav and Murasu, affecting agriculture, coastal infrastructure and other sectors.

During his visit to New Delhi on Tuesday, Naidu met Sitharaman and discussed the state's financial situation, cyclone damage, the Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub, release of Purvodaya funds, region-specific development plans and key decisions announced at the recent CII Partnership Summit in Visakhapatnam.
The Chief Minister explained that preliminary estimates put the combined losses from the two cyclones at over Rs 7,000 crore.
Crops ready for harvest were submerged in floodwaters, severely affecting farmers.
He briefed her on the precautionary measures taken before the cyclones and subsequent relief and restoration operations.
Despite the impact of El Nino, the state had ensured irrigation water supply to several areas through the Pattiseema project.
However, the cyclones dealt a severe blow to farmers.
Coastal infrastructure and, particularly, the power distribution network also suffered extensive damage.

Naidu said Central teams had already visited the state to assess the losses and requested immediate assistance without waiting for prolonged delays, stating that early financial support would help accelerate relief and restoration.
The Chief Minister also outlined region-specific development strategies for Visakhapatnam, Amaravati and Tirupati to drive economic growth.

Regarding the Rayalaseema Horticulture Hub, for which Sitharaman had earlier laid the foundation stone, he sought funds for infrastructure, rural road connectivity, irrigation facilities and promotion of drip irrigation.
He also requested additional Central assistance for the Visakhapatnam Economic Region, which is witnessing rapid growth, to accelerate development and ensure its benefits reach the people.

stories.headline: How Youth and Communities Are Coming Together to Protect Kashmir's Vital Water Commons
stories.title: How Youth and Communities Are Coming Together to Protect Kashmir's Vital Water Commons
stories.summary: River Jhelum, Foot Bridge Srinagar Submerged ankle-deep in the muddy shallows of the Jhelum, Nayeem Farooq pulled a tangled plastic sheet from the water and dropped it into the growing pile beside him. The B-Tech student from Baramulla had begun cleaning the river only two months earlier. Behind him, volunteers carried sacks of waste up the slippery embankment. For Farooq, the river was no longer just a waterway at the edge of town; it had become a responsibility he could no longer ignore. Nayeem farooq and his team collecting the garbage from the Jhelum in polythenes “The Day the Jhelum Became Personal” “I and my cousin were once sitting on the banks of the Jhelum in Baramulla when he went for a swim in the river. But when he returned, his eyes had turned red. Concerned, I asked him what had happened, and he told me that the polluted water had caused irritation and infection. What seemed like an ordinary moment soon became a deeply disturbing experience for me. I could not stop thinking about how a river that sustains an entire town was being pushed towards such neglect”, Nayeem said. “As I began observing its condition more closely, I came across heaps of garbage, discarded diapers and even dead animals dumped into the water. It was heartbreaking to see a river that people depend on for their drinking water being reduced to a dumping ground. I kept wondering how we could allow the very water body that sustains our lives to become a threat to our health. For nearly one-and-a-half years, I had been appealing to people through social media to stop polluting the Jhelum, but the response was far from encouraging. I eventually realised that words alone would not bring change; I had to step forward myself, take responsibility and set an example. That realisation became the beginning of my journey to clean and protect the Jhelum.” Jhelum is Kashmir’s lifeline, supplying drinking water and irrigation while also protecting the Valley from floods. But unchecked pollution, encroachment, and weak conservation have steadily weakened these functions. Originating at Verinag, the river collects water from streams including the Lidder, Veshav, and Rambiara before draining into Wular Lake and flowing out of the Valley. Drains from south to north Kashmir discharge directly into it, while solid waste dumping and illegal sand mining damage its ecology. The loss of wetlands and floodplains has also reduced its capacity to absorb excess water, leaving the Jhelum increasingly vulnerable to flooding after sustained rain. Jhelum Clean Drive: From One Volunteer to a Community Movement Shahida (name changed), a resident of Baramulla, proudly recalled, “While dropping my children to school one morning, I saw Nayeem Farooq and his team cleaning the Jhelum. My children noticed them and asked me what they were doing. I explained that they were cleaning the river to keep our environment clean and protect the water we drink. I was happy to see their curiosity, and they later started sharing the message with their classmates, telling them why it is important to keep our rivers clean. The impact of this initiative is also visible at home. My children no longer tolerate garbage lying around in our garden or inside the house. They make sure everything is kept clean. This initiative has taught them that cleanliness is not just about keeping our homes clean but also about taking responsibility for our surroundings. I feel that when children learn to care for nature at such a young age, they become agents of change and inspire others to do the same.” “I had been raising awareness about river pollution for nearly one-and-a-half years before launching the Jhelum Clean Drive around two-and-a-half months ago. What began as an individual effort has gradually brought together a group of 60 to 75 volunteers, including nearly 35 to 40 women, most of them young people,” Nayeem Farooq said. “Together, we have collected around 11.5 tonnes of garbage from one stretch of the river in Baramulla and transported it to a designated municipal dumping site. The Municipal Council has also extended support to our efforts. Alongside the clean-up drives, we conduct awareness campaigns through social media and local mosques especially on Friday sermons, urging people not to use the river as a dustbin.” “However, cleaning the visible garbage is only the beginning. I am equally concerned about the waste entering the Jhelum through drainage pipes, particularly from butcher shops and other commercial establishments along its banks. Even after cleaning a stretch, I often return the following day to find fresh garbage dumped at the same spot, which can be disheartening. Yet, I believe change takes time and sustained community participation. I have also approached the Deputy Commissioner Baramulla, SyeedFakhrudin Hamid, with an application seeking measures to prevent garbage dumping along the riverbanks and bridges. My aim is not to restrict this initiative to Baramulla; I want to extend it to Srinagar and other parts of Kashmir and work towards protecting our rivers and waterbodies,” he added. Beyond Awareness: Youth Taking Action to Protect Jhelum's Water Commons For Mehak Khursheed, the Jhelum is more than just a river; it is a shared common resource that everyone has a responsibility to protect. A Radio Uri RJ, social activist and hotel management graduate, Mehak travelled from Uri to Baramulla to join Nayeem Farooq’s cleanliness drive, believing that protecting water commons is a collective responsibility that goes beyond geographical boundaries and begins with individual action. Mehak removing the plastic trash from the River Jhelum Since the drive began, I have noticed a positive response. People have started calling me, asking about the initiative and expressing their willingness to participate. I travelled from Uri to Baramulla because I believe protecting the Jhelum is not just the responsibility of Baramulla residents; it belongs to all of us. Just as we keep our homes clean, we must protect our rivers. The government should also install dustbins, put up warning boards and impose fines on those who throw garbage into the river. Awareness is important, but without accountability, lasting change will be difficult. For SadiyaJaved, protecting the Jhelum is not just an environmental concern but a responsibility that the younger generation must embrace. A B.Sc. Biochemistry student from Baramulla, Sadiya joined Nayeem Farooq’s Jhelum Clean Drive after learning about it through social media. She believes awareness must translate into action and that greater public and government participation is essential to protecting Kashmir’s water commons. Sadiya on Jhelum Cleanliness Drive “There is no shortage of awareness in Kashmir, but what we lack is action on the ground. During the drive, we received both appreciation and criticism on social media. Some people questioned what difference a few volunteers could make by collecting garbage, but that did not discourage us. Our efforts also encouraged other people to join the cleaning activities. The government has appreciated our initiative, but we have not received any significant support. If the Municipal Council and the administration actively joined hands with us, the impact could be much greater,” Impact of Climate Change on Jhelum Farooq Ahmed, Executive Engineer, Flood Control Department Kashmir Explains, “Climate change is altering rainfall patterns in Kashmir. Instead of prolonged rainfall, we are increasingly witnessing short-duration, intense rainfall and cloudbursts, leading to sudden fluctuations in water levels, particularly in the Jhelum's tributaries. The Jhelum basin is surrounded by mountainous catchment areas, and water from several tributaries eventually flows into the river, putting pressure on its carrying capacity. We need to treat these catchment areas and restore floodplains and flood basins to better manage flood risks.” “Another major concern is illegal sand mining, which is gradually weakening the river's embankments,” Farooq Ahmed said. “People extract sand from the river, often under the cover of darkness, and in the process damage the flood-protection structures. We do not permit official mining in the Jhelum under our jurisdiction, but illegal extraction remains a challenge. Protecting the river requires collective efforts, strict enforcement and public cooperation.” According to a study “ Assessment and interpretation of surface water quality in Jhelum River and its tributaries using multivariate statistical methods” published in Environmental Monitoring and Assessment reveals water quality in the Jhelum River and its tributaries in the Kashmir Himalayas is consistently deteriorating. The researchers tested 14 physico-chemical parameters at 26 sites across all four seasons and found that the upstream Jhelum was least polluted, while Nallah Sindh had the poorest water quality. They reported that the Jhelum and Wular Lake were strongly affected by pollution from adjoining tributaries, and that chemical, conventional, and organic pollutants were key factors influencing the river’s condition. The study concluded that its findings could help guide the sustainable management of Kashmir’s surface-water resources and protect the region’s fragile ecology. Govt Backs the Initiative Manzoor Moazin, Sanitation Supervisor, Municipal Council Baramulla, said. “We regularly organise cleanliness drives, dedicating an hour to cleaning different areas. We also involve self-help groups, conduct awareness programmes and deploy cleanliness vehicles to maintain sanitation across the town. However, public participation, particularly in Old Town Baramulla and densely populated areas, remains a challenge. There is a need to develop a stronger sense of civic responsibility so that cleanliness becomes a daily habit rather than remaining limited to official drives. I appreciate Nayeem Farooq's efforts and have also been actively participating in his cleanliness campaign. Such initiatives, supported by public participation and government efforts, can bring lasting change in how we protect our rivers and shared spaces.” (The author is a recipient of the Promise of Commons Fellowship 2026, on the significance of Commons and its community stewardship)
